t: Earliest Second to Mark Indices II — Binary Search + Deadline Greedy
o: Each second we may decrement some nums[i], reset nums[changeIndices[s]] to any value, mark a zero-valued index, or idle; we want every index marked as early as possible. Key observation: if index i appears in changeIndices within the first t seconds, we can wait until its **last** occurrence at second d and reset it to 0 for free — costing only 2 seconds total (reset + mark). An index that never appears needs nums[i] decrements plus 1 mark. Feasibility for a horizon t can be checked greedily, and if all indices can be marked within t seconds, so within t+1 (extra room never hurts), so we binary search the answer. Example 1: with t = 6 the three resets land on seconds 1–3 and marks on 4–6.
k: An index appearing in the window costs 2 ops (reset at its last occurrence + mark); a missing index costs nums[i]+1.
Feasibility is monotone in t, enabling binary search on the answer.
Greedy sweep: reserve each last-occurrence second for its reset, spend remaining seconds on decrements first, then pending marks.

a.n: Approach 1: Binary Search on t with Greedy Feasibility Check
a.i: For a horizon t, record the last occurrence of each index. Total demand is D + 2k where D = sum of nums over absent indices and k = number of present indices; if that exceeds t it is infeasible. Otherwise sweep seconds 1..t: at a last-occurrence second perform that reset (adding one pending mark); on other seconds consume a decrement-unit if any remain, else a pending mark. All deadlines are t, so consuming decrements first keeps maximal flexibility; success means both pools drain to zero.
s: Binary search t in [1, m]; check(t):
Compute last[i] = last second ≤ t where i appears in changeIndices.
Let D = Σ nums[i] over absent i, k = count of present i; fail if D + 2k > t.
Sweep s = 1..t: if s is a last occurrence, pending++; else decrement D if positive, else pending. Succeed iff both end at 0.
Return the smallest feasible t, or -1.
a.t: O((n + m) log m) — each feasibility check is a linear sweep, run O(log m) times by binary search.
a.sp: O(n) — the last-occurrence array per check.

w: The heart of the problem is proving the greedy check correct: resetting at the last occurrence dominates decrementing, and with a uniform deadline, draining decrements before marks is safe. Pitfalls: forgetting the mark still costs a separate second after the reset, forgetting 'do nothing' allows slack (use ≤, not ==, on totals — handled by the drain test), and 64-bit sums of nums. Follow-up: return the actual schedule of operations.
